title: When the sangha disappoints
hook: communities have flaws; stay kind, stay honest
tomorrow: how do you check a teacher before you trust one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, being sangha: show up, and lift the heavy pot together. Today, the day the community lets you down.
screen: `SHOW UP.` → `THEN THE COMMUNITY LETS YOU DOWN.`

segments.voice: Every group chat has the day it goes quiet after one message too many. The Thursday sit group near Mai's program met tonight to plan the summer and had that day: two longtime members argued about moving the sit online, one walked out, and Mai sat there holding her tea. Her text afterward was short: i thought Buddhists didn't fight. The texts would disagree with her. They keep the record of a fight that split a whole community of monks, in the city of Kosambi, while the Buddha himself was there.
screen: `ONE MESSAGE TOO MANY.` → `"I THOUGHT BUDDHISTS DIDN'T FIGHT."` → `A SPLIT AT KOSAMBI.`

segments.voice: It started small, a dispute over whether one monk had broken a rule. Then sides formed, and the monks wounded each other with words. The Buddha asked them to stop, and they told him, in effect, to stay out of it. So he spoke verses on hatred and went off to stay alone in a forest. One line, in Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love". And the story doesn't end there. The lay people of Kosambi stopped bowing to the quarreling monks and stopped feeding them, until the monks made peace. That's the Buddhist answer. The sangha is a refuge, and it's made of people, so the texts tell its fights honestly and give it ways back: admitting a fault out loud, forgiving, refusing to feed a grudge. Now a neighbor. In the Torah, the commandment says "nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people", and Jewish teaching on Yom Kippur says that wrongs between people are mended only when you go to the person and set it right. The shared part is real: don't carry a grudge inside your own community. The difference is honest too. The Torah grounds it in God's command; the verse ends, I am the LORD. The Dhammapada grounds it in how hatred itself works, and calls that an old rule.
screen: `A SMALL DISPUTE, THEN SIDES.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE VILLAGE STOPS FEEDING THE FIGHT.` · `A NEIGHBOR: BEAR NO GRUDGE.` · then, large: `FLAWED AND DEAR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one group you belong to that has let you down: a team, a family chat, a congregation. Say the line softly out loud, once: hatred does not cease by hatred. Then sit and let that group come to mind as it is, flawed, and part of your life.
When the sangha disappoints: the day the community fails you, and the old ways back, admitting, forgiving, and letting the grudge go hungry.
Your line: flawed and dear. A grudge can't live long if nobody feeds it. Seventeen days of the block, kept.

screen: `DAY 1742 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 17 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: HOW DO YOU CHECK A TEACHER BEFORE YOU TRUST ONE?`

howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities hold regular gatherings where monks and nuns admit faults to one another and settle disputes by set procedures; lay Buddhists recite the Dhammapada's verses on hatred and are taught to reconcile rather than nurse a grudge.

notes: Kosambi quarrel paraphrased from Vinaya Mahavagga X and MN 128: a dispute over whether a monk had committed an offense; factions; the Buddha's appeals rebuffed ('let the Blessed One live at ease... we will be known for this quarrel'); he speaks verses on hatred (MN 128 includes the line on enmity not appeased by enmity) and goes to stay alone (the Parileyyaka forest in the Vinaya). The lay people of Kosambi withholding respect and alms until reconciliation is from Mahavagga X.5; confirm. No counts (e.g., how many times he asked) given on purpose.

Dhammapada 5 quoted from Max Müller 1881 ('For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule'); the script quotes the middle and paraphrases 'old rule'. Confirm exact wording and punctuation.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Leviticus 19:18 quoted from JPS 1917 ('nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people'); please verify the JPS 1917 wording (KJV has the same phrase). 'I am the LORD' ends the verse in both. The Yom Kippur line paraphrases Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (Yom Kippur atones for wrongs between people only once one has appeased the other). Shared: not carrying a grudge inside one's own community. Difference: the Torah grounds it in God's command; the Dhammapada in how hatred works ('an old rule'). Neither ranked; a Jewish reviewer should confirm the framing.

Shape: wisdom. Mai's storyline: the Thursday sit group's weeknight planning meeting argues about moving online; one member walks out. (The monthly unity beat with Ava's family was day 1728; the next is planned for 1749.)
Surprising fact: in the Kosambi story, lay people ended the monks' quarrel by refusing to feed it.
